question: Why do we run lab tests and checks for patients in the intensive care unit (ICU)?

options.A: To replace the standard physical assessment entirely
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of hospital stays
options.C: To track how well current treatments are working
options.D: To shorten the nursing shift handover time

explanation: Think of lab tests and diagnostics as your patient's report card. They give us real-time clues to see if our care is helping or if things are taking a turn. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h1)

question: In critical care, why do we need constant monitoring alongside regular physical checks?

options.A: Doctors rarely visit the intensive care unit more than once a day
options.B: Physical assessments are completely useless in critical care
options.C: Hospital accreditation standards legally demand constant monitoring
options.D: They experience rapid and unpredictable physiological shifts

explanation: Critical care patients can change in a matter of minutes! Continuous monitoring helps you catch hidden trouble early before it becomes a bigger crisis. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h1)

question: Where do we usually place a peripheral arterial line?
explanation: The radial artery at the wrist is our go-to spot because it is easy to reach and has great backup blood supply (collateral circulation). [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h2)

question: Why must a nurse line up the pressure monitor with the phlebostatic axis before reading blood pressure numbers?

options.A: To keep the electronic monitor screen from turning off
options.B: To prevent false high or false low pressure readings
options.C: To make sure the blood sample does not get contaminated
options.D: To stop the arterial line from forming a blood clot

explanation: Leveling the transducer to the right atrium means gravity won't trick your monitor into giving you fake high or low numbers. Accuracy matters! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the normal pH range for human arterial blood?
explanation: Keep this number locked in your memory! A pH of 7.35 to 7.45 keeps body enzymes working smoothly and cells happy. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does a high PaCO2 level on an arterial blood gas (ABG) report usually tell you?

options.A: Inadequate ventilation or carbon dioxide retention
options.B: Excessive bicarbonate production by the liver
options.C: Too much oxygen being delivered by the ventilator
options.D: Rapid breathing caused by severe emotional anxiety

explanation: If the lungs aren't blowing off air well enough, carbon dioxide builds up in the blood, driving that PaCO2 level right up. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does a rising serum lactate level usually mean for a sick patient?

options.A: Red blood cells are multiplying too quickly in the bone marrow
options.B: The patient is eating too many carbohydrates in their tube feeding
options.C: The kidneys are filtering waste products much faster than normal
options.D: Tissues are not getting enough oxygen and are using anaerobic metabolism

explanation: When cells are starved of oxygen, they switch to an emergency backup energy system that leaves behind lactic acid as waste. High lactate = cells need oxygen! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which lab test is our best friend for spotting heart muscle damage?
explanation: Troponin is a special protein found inside heart muscle. When the heart gets hurt, troponin leaks out into the bloodstream for us to spot on labs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the big advantage of using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) right at the bedside?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for blood tests and lab work
options.B: It removes all risk of infection during invasive procedures
options.C: It gives immediate answers at the bedside without moving the patient
options.D: It produces permanent color photographs without using sound waves

explanation: POCUS lets you peek inside and check organs instantly without having to transport a fragile patient out of the unit. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h5)

question: What do we mean when we say an ultrasound is 'operator-dependent'?

options.A: The machine will not turn on unless a licensed physician is in the room
options.B: The accuracy of the results depends heavily on the skill of the person holding the probe
options.C: Patients must pay a separate fee every time the probe touches their skin
options.D: The device requires constant maintenance by an external technician

explanation: Because you have to guide the probe yourself, the picture and diagnosis depend a lot on your scanning technique and practice! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is one of the biggest risks when wheeling a critical patient away for an advanced scan?

options.A: Permanent discoloration of the patient's skin
options.B: Accidental dislodgement of breathing tubes and lines
options.C: Automatic deletion of electronic health records
options.D: Sudden freezing of the hospital computed tomography machine

explanation: Moving beds down hallways and shifting patients onto imaging tables puts a lot of stress on delicate IV lines and breathing tubes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h6)

question: You are getting a ventilated, unstable patient ready for a CT scan. What is your most important safety check?

options.A: Turning off all continuous intravenous drug infusions to save battery life
options.B: Ensuring portable oxygen, monitor, and emergency equipment are fully functional
options.C: Removing all patient identification bands to prevent scanning delays
options.D: Notifying the hospital cafeteria that the patient will miss lunch

explanation: Always make sure your transport life support gear is fully charged and working so you are ready for anything while away from the ICU. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h6)

question: What does an electroencephalogram (EEG) actually measure in a sick patient?

options.D: Blood flow through the carotid arteries

explanation: Think of an EEG as a way to listen in on the brain's electrical chatter to spot things like seizures or abnormal brain wave patterns. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is keeping an eye on intracranial pressure (ICP) so vital after a severe head injury?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing chronic back pain
options.B: To determine when the patient is ready for solid foods
options.C: To calculate the exact number of calories the brain burns daily
options.D: To make sure enough blood flows to the brain despite swelling

explanation: When the brain swells inside the skull, high pressure can pinch blood vessels closed and cut off vital oxygen. Monitoring helps us prevent brain starvation. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT something a bedside nurse is supposed to do during diagnostic tests?

options.A: Performing the official radiological interpretation of the scan
options.B: Monitoring the patient's vital signs throughout the procedure
options.C: Checking the insertion site for bleeding afterward
options.D: Verifying that informed consent has been obtained

explanation: Reading and officially interpreting scans is the job of trained radiologists or doctors, though nurses definitely watch for patient safety! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h8)

question: Why do nurses need to watch a patient closely after they get IV contrast dye for a scan?

options.A: To watch for delayed allergic reactions and kidney stress
options.B: To measure how fast the dye exits through sweat glands
options.C: To prevent the intravenous site from leaking sterile water
options.D: To ensure the patient does not fall asleep too quickly

explanation: Contrast dye can sometimes trigger sneaky allergic reactions or put extra stress on the kidneys, so post-procedure monitoring is a must. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T3#GNS321_U2_T3_h8)
